items.originalTitle: The Nice Ones review – invasion of the sunny personality snatchers
items.author: Phil Hoad
items.title: The Nice Ones review – invasion of the sunny personality snatchers
items.summary: Peter Stylianou’s watchably unsettling tale of unbalanced minds and Unidentified Aerial Phenomena does its best to please Drone shots are two-a-penny in cinema these days, but it’s a mark of this £80,000 British indie sci-fi’s visual astuteness that it largely avoids them in a film plagued by drone-like entities. Instead, it takes a suggestive approach: protagonist Kate (Joelle Rae) is staring out of the window on a car journey, up into the night sky, when a pinprick of light flares out before shooting out a laser towards the ground – then darting off into a cloudbank. Kate chews over this anomaly with boyfriend Dale (Emrhys Cooper), en route to a get-together of his old uni gang in a countryside Airbnb. Already not at ease among his mates, Kate gets a ribbing when she repeats her UFO story (or Unidentified Aerial Phenomena, as they are called these days). And there are knowing glances about her psychiatric history: she once fended off an abusive boyfriend at knifepoint, insisting he was possessed. But if she is delusional, then it seems to be spreading: her one ally, spacey teacher Shelly (Ayvianna Snow), re-enters the room after a suspiciously long fag break, marvelling about how they will all imminently join “the light”.

items.originalTitle: ‘Partly the movie’s fault I’m a writer at all’: why Wonder Boys is my feelgood movie
items.author: Duncan Riddell
items.title: ‘Partly the movie’s fault I’m a writer at all’: why Wonder Boys is my feelgood movie
items.summary: The latest in our series of writers picking their most comforting rewatches is a tribute to Curtis Hanson’s insightful 2000 comedy drama I’m allergic to movies and books about writers. Washed-up novelists, aspiring screenwriters, creative writing professors in the throes of a midlife crisis who cheat on their wives – take your pick. Chalk it up to my being a writer who for two decades wrote continually and fruitlessly about writers. And yet, I love Wonder Boys, Curtis Hanson’s 2000 comedy drama about a rumpled creative writing professor who can’t seem to finish his second novel and is having an affair with his boss’s wife. It’s partly the movie’s fault I’m a writer at all. I saw Wonder Boys on its opening weekend, when I was 17, and the notion of poring over novels with kindred spirits in a sun-dappled seminar room at some leafy liberal arts college – where I’d find myself a year later – held endless appeal. Even the misadventures of the film’s professor, Grady Tripp (Michael Douglas, never better), seemed romantic to me. On the eve of his university’s annual literary festival, Grady’s wife leaves him. His lover, Sara, announces she’s pregnant with his child. And James Leer, his brilliant but troubled student, who can rattle off Hollywood suicides in alphabetical order, shows up at the festival’s kick-off party cradling what may or may not be a cap gun. Grady responds to all this with the urgency of a veteran pot smoker – which he is.

items.originalTitle: Democrats Call for Probe Into Military Leaders as U.S. Army Whistleblower Alleges Warnings Were Dismissed Ahead of Deadly Iran Attack
items.author: Miranda Jeyaretnam
items.title: Democrats Call for Probe Into Military Leaders as U.S. Army Whistleblower Alleges Warnings Were Dismissed Ahead of Deadly Iran Attack
items.summary: U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth salutes as a U.S. Army carry team moves a flag-draped transfer case containing the remains of Sgt. 1st Class Noah L. Tietjens at Dover Air Force Base in Delaware on March 7, 2026. —Roberto Schmidt—Getty Images An American soldier has alleged that U.S. military leaders dismissed concerns ahead of an Iranian attack that killed six servicemembers on March 1. The complaint, submitted Friday to the House and Senate Armed Services committees and first reported by CBS on Sunday, alleges that U.S. Army leaders did not heed warnings about thin fortifications at a command post at Kuwait’s Port Shuaiba. Iran launched a retaliatory drone attack on the command post a day after the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Feb. 28. It remains the deadliest attack on American troops since 2021. Over the eight months of the war, a total of 23 U.S. servicemembers have died . Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom, who filed the complaint and was among the dozens wounded in the attack, called the event a “tactical failure” by “the Army, our leadership, and myself.” Ramsbottom said he had twice raised concerns about the lack of protection from aerial attacks to his superiors but was told, “We don’t have to worry about protection.” He said in an interview with CBS that a counter-drone system “never arrived at Shuaiba and we don’t know if it was ever even ordered to or requested.” He also alleged that the post had “no physician, no fixed aid station, and only one ambulance.” A day after the attack, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the command post suffered casualties despite its fortifications not because of a lack of preparedness. “Every once in a while you might have one, unfortunately, we call it a squirter that makes its way through [air defenses]. And in that particular case it happened to hit a tactical operations center that was fortified,” Hegseth said at a press conference. “But these are powerful weapons.” The Pentagon announced an investigation into the attack on March 3, and the Associated Press reported that it had concluded in June, with a private briefing to families of the slain servicemembers in July. The findings of the investigation have not been publicly disclosed, although widow Michelle Tietjens told CBS that officials acknowledged no mistakes. Ramsbottom’s attorneys separately requested an independent investigation into the attack after filing his Nov. 13 complaint. TIME has reached out to the Pentagon and U.S. Central Command for comment. Disputed accounts Around a week before the U.S. and Israel launched their attacks on Iran, around 70 members of the U.S. Army’s 103rd Sustainment Command were relocated from Camp Arifjan, a major U.S. base south of Kuwait City, to the smaller outpost at Port of Shuaiba. Days after the war began, Hegseth told reporters that the Defense Department prioritized protecting U.S. troops and moving “the vast majority … off the X, out of the range of Iranian fire.” The facility, situated in the civilian port on Kuwait’s southern coast, was within range of Iranian missiles. The Washington Post reported in July that military leaders had ignored intelligence warnings that the post was a probable Iranian target. CBS reported in March that the post was surrounded by T-walls, steel-reinforced concrete barriers that provide protection from mortars and rockets. Ramsbottom told Colorado news station KOAA in April that the facility was protected from “legacy threats” like mortar fire and car bombs, but not from modern aerial attacks, such as by drones or missiles. Other survivors of the attack told CBS in April that the unit “was unprepared to provide any defense for itself. It was not a fortified position.” One soldier described the fort as “a bunch of little tin buildings where we can set up makeshift offices.” The Post reported that a 2021 photograph showed what appeared to be a thin metal rooftop over the building, although it was not clear whether any reinforcement existed underneath. Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell rejected reporting that the position was not well-protected. “A Tactical Operations Center is not a ‘makeshift office space.’ The secure facility was fortified with 6-foot walls,” he posted on March 3. “Every possible measure has been taken to safeguard our troops — at every level,” Parnell wrote. Multiple news outlets previously reported that no sirens sounded to alert troops before the deadly strike. CBS reported in March that sirens had occasionally gone off after a drone had already entered the base in previous incidents. CBS reported in April that incoming missile alarms had sounded several hours before the attack, alerting around 60 troops to take cover when a ballistic missile flew overhead, and that an all-clear alert had sounded around 30 minutes before the Iranian drone hit. Troops told the outlet that officers had removed their helmets and resumed work at their desks after the all-clear alert. Soldiers told the Post that the threat warning system was initially not working when a team was sent to scout the post before troops were relocated there. They said repairs had been made to get it operational before the strike happened. U.S. Army Central previously said in statements to media outlets that the alarm system at the facility was working at the time of the attack. Democrats call for probe The whistleblower complaint adds fuel to the fire as Democrats plan to launch congressional investigations into the Trump Administration’s handling of the war when they take control of both chambers of Congress in January. In September, Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Rep. Pat Ryan of New York called for public hearings, citing earlier whistleblower reports about delayed medical care for wounded servicemembers, mistreatment of families, and concerns around the Army’s investigation into the attack. Rep. Maggie Goodlander of New Hampshire described the handling of the attack as “a profound failure of leadership” and said “the Pentagon cannot be allowed to stonewall Congress.” Democrats and some Republicans have also called for Hegseth to step down or face impeachment , and the latest allegations are likely to intensify scrutiny of his leadership. Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D, Conn.), the ranking member on the Senate’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, reportedly sent a letter on Sunday to the Pentagon requesting a classified briefing with Hegseth and “all force protection assessments” for the post. “I’m again demanding full disclosure about the Port Shuaiba attack—an accounting of misjudgments by political appointees likely led to increased vulnerability & greater casualties,” Blumenthal posted on social media on Sunday night. “The families of the six fallen servicemembers, the wounded survivors, & the American people deserve full transparency & accountability,” he added in another post . “It is time for a reckoning.”

items.originalTitle: Poll: Republicans have a MAGA dilemma after their midterm losses
items.author: Erin Doherty
items.title: Poll: Republicans have a MAGA dilemma after their midterm losses
items.summary: The Republican Party’s midterm wipeout has torn apart President Donald Trump’s coalition. For months, polling has shown cracks among Trump’s 2024 voters over immigration , the Iran war and the president’s influence. Now, new results from The POLITICO Poll , conducted just days after the election, reveal a deep chasm between Trump’s self-identified MAGA base and the non-MAGA voters who helped fuel his return to the White House. The two camps hold sharply different interpretations of the GOP’s historic midterm defeat and what comes next for their party, according to the survey conducted by PF Global. MAGA Trump loyalists were more likely to say the president is not to blame for the losses — that things would have gone better if he was on the ballot — and that the party should now move closer to Trump. Non-MAGA Trump voters starkly disagreed, saying they are ready to move away from him and his unpopular agenda. About one in five said they voted for Democratic candidates this cycle. The fault line is a fresh warning sign that Republicans, desperate to stitch back together a winning coalition after their midterm calamity, may struggle to keep the voters that powered Trump’s victory in 2024 in the fold. And it calls into question just how loyal the party should be to a leader — and movement — it has spent the last decade united around. Overall, just over half of all Trump voters said the president will be able to make a comeback from the election losses. “As the [GOP] spends the next two years figuring out who it is and what it stands for, these divisions will only be further exposed,” said Republican strategist Doug Heye. Here are four charts that show just how much the midterms have divided Trump’s own voters. A majority of non-MAGA Trump voters blamed Republicans' loss of the House and the Senate on Trump’s actions since taking office, with far fewer saying the campaigns themselves were responsible. A 59% majority also said the president is a loser of the midterms, a striking rebuke from a group of voters who helped his return to the White House. But MAGA Trump voters are torn over who they blame for their losses. The divide mirrors disagreements happening at the top levels of the Republican Party. In the immediate aftermath of the election, some Republicans, at least tepidly, began pointing fingers at the president. Others have called for a “reckoning” without explicitly laying the blame at Trump’s feet or articulating an alternative vision for the GOP. “There is no way to sugarcoat what happened on Election Day. From coast to coast, and in some of the reddest parts of the country, Republicans were humiliated,” 31 Republican National Committee members wrote in a letter to GOP lawmakers this week. Trump, who ahead of the midterms repeatedly urged voters to “pretend” he was on the ballot, insisted in a Truth Social post after the election that, “I JUST WASN’T ON THE BALLOT. IF I WERE, WE WOULD HAVE WON IN A LANDSLIDE!” “President Trump will never stop delivering results for the American people and he will undoubtedly go down as the most successful and consequential president in American history,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement. As Republican Party leaders grapple with how to rebound from the midterms, MAGA isn’t ready to move on from Trump: They said the path forward is embracing Trump and his agenda. Non-MAGA Trump voters said the opposite — and nearly half of them think their Republican candidates should have broken with the president on the economy this cycle. “It is very clear that Election Day 2026 was an unequivocal rebuke of Donald Trump, both him personally and his policies,” said one national GOP operative who worked on midterm races, granted anonymity to speak candidly about the landscape. “MAGA needs a serious rebrand if it is going to have any success in the future.” That presents a complicated picture for Republican leaders, who will have to find a way to appeal to Trump’s fiercely loyal MAGA base without alienating the less committed voters who helped deliver his 2024 victory. On Election Night, as the scale of Republican losses was becoming clear, POLITICO asked GOP operatives who worked on midterm races whether the defeat meant it was time for Republicans to consider a new vision for the party. “How can it not be?” one person responded. It’s “the worst defeat a party has taken in 50 years.” Non-MAGA Trump voters are split over whether Trump can make a comeback after the midterms bloodbath. MAGA, however, is quite confident in the president’s abilities to do so. And collectively, Trump voters are more optimistic about the Republican Party than the president. Some key aspects of Trump’s agenda are unpopular with Americans, including his push for mass deportations, tariffs imposed on key trade partners and the war in Iran. The congressional Republicans who once supported many of those policies are now weighing whether they can distance themselves to regain voters’ trust. In an interview with “ 60 Minutes ” after the midterms, Trump admitted his party’s losses may be attributed at least in part to the Iran war and the resulting high gas prices — though he also mentioned how, in some cases, voters “didn’t like the candidates” and asserted, again, that he wasn’t on the ballot. "President Trump remains the unequivocal leader of our party who's cut taxes, lowered drug costs and secured our border,” RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre said in a statement. “Republicans will continue to harness his ability to energize our base and expose the Democrats' disastrous record to win back our majorities in 2028." As the party looks ahead to 2028, Republicans are already weighing how much the party’s next presidential nominee should carry the MAGA mantle. Some Hill Republicans are increasingly warming to the prospect of a Marco Rubio presidential bid, arguing that voters may be looking for a new direction after Trump — and Vice President JD Vance may be too closely tied to the president’s agenda. MAGA Trump voters said decisively that they prefer someone who has worked in the administration — another sign of their support for the president, and of the difficulty of changing course as a party given that loyalty. “I think everybody reserves the right to adjust. You know, learn from this,” GOP Rep. and incoming Oklahoma Sen. Kevin Hern recently told POLITICO . Asked his favorite candidate of the three he expected to run: Vance, Rubio or DeSantis, he replied with a smile: “Everybody.”

items.originalTitle: What Are Your Odds of Winning New York’s Affordable Housing Lottery?
items.author: Samantha Maldonado
items.title: What Are Your Odds of Winning New York’s Affordable Housing Lottery?
items.summary: Good news: You almost certainly have better odds of winning the New York City affordable housing lottery than of getting audited — a 1 in 1,101 chance — or getting bitten by a city dog, a 1 in 2,222 chance. And you’ve got way better odds of winning a lottery apartment than nabbing one of those Knicks-themed wastebaskets the Sanitation Department gave out in June. Just five people snagged one, out of 125,000 who applied, putting the odds at 1 in 25,000. Meanwhile, the chances of winning New York City’s coveted and frustrating affordable housing lottery for any one application have been 1 in 510, according to The City Reporter’s analysis of a two-year span using public data. In that time period, the city received 10,250,872 applications and, of that pool, 20,200 households ultimately signed a lease for an affordable, rent-stabilized lottery apartment. In real world terms, the odds look like this: If everyone in five full subway cars — which carry about 100 people each — applied to Housing Connect, just one straphanger would have won an apartment in the group. “It’s crazy,” said Brad Greenburg, executive director of the NYU Furman Center, a real estate think tank. “A lot of people apply for more than one [lottery], so it’s not like one person has a 1 in 510 chance necessarily of getting a unit — they might have a much better chance than that.” Read our full series on New York City’s affordable housing lottery. The housing lottery is not the only way to find an affordable apartment in New York City, but it is the most accessible option for New Yorkers who are not eligible for, unable to access or don’t want to use other forms of taxpayer-funded housing help, such as rental vouchers or traditional public housing. In an opaque and complicated system that garners millions of applications a year from New Yorkers desperate to find a stable and affordable place to live, 1 in 510 are the rough odds. (Read our methodology on how we calculated the odds and why we are confident in our findings.) But the devil’s in the details, and an applicant’s chances can climb or fall steeply based on factors like household income and where they apply. Frustratingly for those who need affordable housing the most, your chances of winning a lottery apartment were better if you earned more money, according to lottery data compiled between January 2022 and October 2024 and by law submitted by the Department of Housing Preservation and Development to the City Council. This trend was also true when our newsroom first analyzed housing lottery data in 2020. The households with the worst odds of all, in the “low income” category — which at the time of the data analyzed was between roughly $78,000 and $124,240 for a family of four — had a roughly 1 in 639 chance of winning, meaning there were 639 applications for every one apartment available in that group. But in the higher income categories, dubbed “moderate” and “middle” income, the chances were almost twice as good: 1 in 325 and 1 in 398, respectively. Across those two categories, the incomes for applicants spanned about $124,240 to $256,245 for a family of four, depending on the size of the household. At the same time, of the 20,200 signed leases in the two years analyzed, the majority were awarded to people who were listed in the lowest economic income groups. Roughly 30% or just under 6,000 applicants who signed leases were in the extremely low income category. Those tenants earned $32,610 for a single person or $46,590 for a family of four. MORE: What is Area Median Income? The Magic Number Behind Affordable Housing Math in NYC Applicants considered very low income made up roughly a third of the overall leases. These applicants typically made up to $54,350 for a single person or $77,650 for a family of four. And nearly 24% or 4,735 applicants who categorized as low income won a housing lottery. They made up to $86,960 for a single person or $124,240 for a family of four. That means that the majority of housing lottery leases were awarded to New Yorkers who make less than about $90,000. Amira Willingham, who works in e-commerce marketing, felt like she beat the odds in early 2024 when she moved into a Chelsea studio she’d applied to the year before. She was in the low income category, the group with the lowest odds, according to The City Reporter’s analysis. It took years of trying before her number hit. “ As soon as the clock struck on my 18th birthday, I started applying,” the now 25-year-old said. “I was ready to move to any borough, any apartment size.” Five years passed without luck, but then in 2023 she got a call back for the Chelsea studio. The rent was $1,329. “There’s literally no world in which I’d be able to live alone for the rent I have,” Willingham said. She previously paid about the same to live with three roommates, and her current building has a rooftop pool, a gym and outdoor terraces. More Choice for the Wealthiest Among the lottery applicants earning the most, the odds of winning were the best. That’s because there are relatively more apartments available for higher-income applicants, fewer of those applicants competing for the units and more choice for those applicants in the form of traditional, market-rate apartments. “If you’re a renter of that [higher] income you would have market options in a range of neighborhoods,” said Rachel Fee, executive director of the New York Housing Conference, an affordable housing policy nonprofit. “If you’re below 80% [Area Median Income], you’re really priced out of most available housing in New York City.” Patrick Boyle, senior policy director at Enterprise Community Partners, a nonprofit that helps arrange affordable housing financing, said the numbers speak to a staggering amount of demand, even when the odds at one income tier appear better than another. “One in 325 is still pretty long odds,” he said. “Those numbers just highlight that there’s tremendous demand across all income brackets.” Sometimes, applicants in the higher-income groups make a decision unthinkable to many New Yorkers: They win the housing lottery, then turn it down. Across all income groups, roughly 2,698 applicants rejected a unit, according to the data — most of them by residents in the low income category. Shay O’Reilly, a nonprofit worker, was one of them. Several years ago, he won a two-bedroom lottery apartment in Flatbush but ultimately said no, in large part because at the time the $2,400 rent was higher than rent-stabilized places on the open market. “We decided not to go for it just because we were like, ‘We can probably find something that’s cheaper,’ and we did,” O’Reilly said. “In 2020, we ended up moving into a two-bedroom, much closer to Prospect Park.” The rent at the time for that place, he said, was $2,000. Preferences in the Lottery In spite of the hurdles and the cumbersome process to get approved, when applications to the housing lottery are selected, it’s random. “There is no favoritism. I keep hearing, ‘You got to know somebody who knows somebody,’ or ‘Pay something under the table’ — all kinds of nonsense. But that’s not true. It really isn’t,” said Charmaine Marizan, affordable housing marketing and leasing manager at Fifth Avenue Committee. “It’s a very stringent, fair, highly supervised process by the city of New York.” But there are factors that add weight to certain applicants within the random lottery, and those built-in preferences influence the odds. Lotteries often include preferences for certain groups, including city employees, people with disabilities and public housing residents. Of the more than 2 million municipal employee applicants, 3,730 signed leases, giving them an overall chance of 1 in 564. For NYCHA residents, the odds are some of the highest out of subcategories. Of the 44,702 NYCHA residents who applied to the lottery, no more than 255 households signed a lease. Those odds are roughly 1 in 182. Across racial groups, the applicants who identified themselves as Pacific Islanders had the best odds: 1 in 444. Meanwhile, the odds for Hispanic residents were roughly 1 in 591; for Black New Yorkers, it was 1 in 524; while white New Yorkers saw odds of 1 in 481. Asian New Yorkers’ odds were 1 in 467 and Native Americans’ odds were 1 in 570. Some applicants chose not to disclose their race. Their odds were 1 in 568. The lottery also has a special boost for applicants from the community district where the apartments are located. That last rule, known as “community preference,” used to set aside half of all lottery apartments for locals, but since the settlement of a federal lawsuit challenging the practice , the preference set-aside has dropped dramatically. Community preference gives an applicant a much better shot at signing a lease. The City Reporter’s analysis found that, with community preference in the time period analyzed, an applicant’s odds are about 1 in 53, whereas without community preference, the odds are 1 in 1,051. Speaking of location, there are huge variations among neighborhoods as to where there are affordable apartments. For example, the community districts that include Long Island City, Williamsburg and Greenpoint Downtown Brooklyn, East New York and the South Bronx were home to the greatest number of affordable apartments since 2020, according to an analysis of HPD advertised lottery data . “That’s where all of the affordable housing is being built, and then places like Bay Ridge have not historically produced very many income-restricted units, if any,” Greenburg said. Lower Incomes, Greater Demand, Less Inventory The levels of affordability of the housing that appears on Housing Connect shape who can apply in the first place. There were more apartments geared towards families making more money in a six year period, the analysis of advertised lottery data shows. From July 2020 to November 2, 2026, just 4% of the 56,271 advertised apartments available on Housing Connect were designated for extremely low-income households. Meanwhile, advertised lotteries for middle-income households made up 39%. The clientele of the organization, which is located in the Northwest Bronx, is typically extremely low income, making under $25,000 per household. “One of the biggest complaints we continue to hear: most of what’s available on Housing Connect is not available for me,” Abrahamson said. “We’re working with people that are at the bottom of the [income] column.” That means there is great demand for inventory built for households on the lower end of the income spectrum. Take one lottery for 45 affordable apartments in Park Slope, Brooklyn. The new building was located on bustling Fifth Avenue and close to the Barclays Center, and its affordable apartments had rent set between $654 for a studio and $2,872 for a two-bedroom. (That is, geared toward very low-income to moderate-income households.) More than 100,000 applicants entered the lottery — most in the first two weeks of the 60-day application period, which closed in December 2025. “I’ve been doing this a long time, and I’ve never seen those numbers that fast. I was amazed,” said Marizan, of the Fifth Avenue Committee, which oversaw the lottery. While only qualified applicants — those whose household size and income match the requirements — should apply, the process of whittling down from the full applicant pool to the people who are verified as eligible to then sign leases can be complicated. All the information an applicant includes in their application must be manually confirmed when and if an applicant’s number is picked in the lottery. That process is onerous, time-consuming and frustrating for both the potential tenant and the lottery specialists trying to match apartments with people, as The City Reporter detailed in our guide on what happens when you go through the lottery. Lots of people get that first call back, but very few actually sign a lease. In the case of the Park Slope building, Marizan’s team looked at 500 applicants within different categories. All 45 households they selected signed leases. When It Works Other reasons for missing out on an apartment can be maddeningly slight: A missing document, or income just over or under the limit. That’s what happened to Dutch de Carvalho, an arts educator, professional dancer and content creator who had been applying to the housing lottery for years; at one point, he counted filling out 196 applications. When he finally got a call back for an apartment, he waited for months to be told he was $400 short on income — and ineligible. “I got rejected at the last minute,” he said. But later that year when the native Manhattanite got a different call back for another lottery apartment — after five months of paperwork — he signed a lease and moved in. “It’s really life changing,” he said. “I’m not worried every month about if I can pay my rent. I’m able to help out my family.” When he shared the news about the apartment on his feed it went super-viral. His first video drew 1.1 million views; a subsequent apartment tour has drawn 9.8 million. “People who live in our city are desperate for affordable housing and our city government does not make it easy to understand the affordable housing process,” de Carvalho told The City Reporter. “I think when people are able to hear first-hand accounts of what it is like to apply, the steps involved, etc. and actually see someone receive a unit, it’s going to spark interest.” Content about the lottery, including tips, tricks and advice from those who won, has an avid audience. The Reddit community for discussing it, r/nychousinglottery , has 25,000 visitors a week. The hashtag #nychousinglottery on TikTok has more than 20 million views. In Chelsea, as thrilled at Willingham is with her affordable studio, she thinks maybe she can hit the lottery twice. She’s continued applying to other Housing Connect apartments in the hopes of leveling up: her sights are on a one-bedroom in Brooklyn. “It doesn’t always work for everybody,” she said, “but when it works, it really works.” Additional reporting by Haidee Chu. items.originalTitle: From the Ground Up: Here’s What It Takes to Build, Build, Build Affordable Housing
items.author: Samantha Maldonado
items.title: From the Ground Up: Here’s What It Takes to Build, Build, Build Affordable Housing
items.summary: Facing down New York’s housing crisis, city leaders of all stripes are pushing three words: build, build, build. But building affordable housing is a complex and time-consuming process. But it takes years of work, millions of dollars and countless hours traversing red tape before new apartments are ready for tenants. As part of The City Reporter’s series on the New York City affordable housing lottery, we took a look at a fairly typical 100% affordable housing project in The Bronx to show exactly what goes into making a new building like this one real — even before it’s listed on Housing Connect. New York City severely needs to build more affordable housing, and those in power feel the crunch. On his first day in office, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he’d quicken the pace. The day he took office, he convened a Streamlining Procedures to Expedite Equitable Development (SPEED) Task Force, whose recommendations promised to slash eight months from the time it takes to build affordable housing by focusing on interagency communication, financing, permitting, construction and lease-ups. On the state level, Gov. Kathy Hochul and the Legislature also reformed the environmental permitting process to accelerate housing development. Read our full series on New York City’s affordable housing lottery. At Twin Parks Terrace , a 182-unit complex in The Bronx’s Fordham Heights, here’s what it took to transform a parking lot into the 14-story affordable apartment building: navigating multiple agencies, $81 million and almost a decade of work. The project went, by all accounts, as smoothly as anyone could hope. “There are no easy sites in New York. Things go from difficult to nightmare, and this was not a nightmare of a project,” said Eli Weiss, principal at Joy Construction, which oversaw the project with Settlement Housing Fund. The process by which Twin Parks Terrace came to fruition is not representative of all affordable housing projects, and if it was built now, it would benefit from some of the changes happening at the local and state levels. But it is a good example of a subsidized, fully affordable housing project built on city land and relying on common financing options. “The journey for any project is many years,” said Emily Lehman, Settlement’s vice president of real estate, who formerly worked at the city housing department for more than a decade. “The timelines we saw for this particular project might look different for a project that was awarded today. 2017: The proposed idea The city Department of Housing Preservation and Development and NYCHA formally asked developers to come up with ideas for building 100% affordable housing on a NYCHA-owned parking lot in The Bronx. Settlement Housing Fund and Joy Construction were among the development teams that submitted a proposal with their affordable housing concept. The submission included the team’s vision for the site, proposed financing, designs, plans for property management and more details. The team met with the agencies to answer questions and talk through the idea. 2018: The concept gets a green light HPD and NYCHA decided to move forward with Settlement’s proposal. The development team celebrated, and then they got to work. So began what is called the “predevelopment timeline,” where several processes happen simultaneously so that everything is ready to put shovels in the ground as soon as the team locks down financing. Danois Architects started advancing the project’s designs, which needed approvals from HPD and the Department of Buildings. Meanwhile, environmental review took place, which analyzed impacts on air quality and noise, among other conditions. There was a mountain of paperwork to fill out and submit to various entities, including reviews for compliance and integrity. Affordable housing development Twin Parks Terrace in the Bronx’s Fordham Heights neighborhood was built on the site of a former public lot, March 11, 2026. Credit: Ben Fractenberg/THE CITY At the same time, the team figured out how to finance the project with dollars from multiple sources. The general contractor priced out the project’s construction, a process that influenced both the financing side and the designs, too. The financing included tax-exempt bond financing from the city Housing Development Corporation and subsidies from HPD. The team also used a federal Low Income Housing Tax Credit and a bank letter of credit, and they received $1.5 million in capital subsidies from local officials. Each financing partner had a checklist with hundreds of requirements for the team to complete. “I remember at the time saying that my checklists were having baby checklists,” said Judy Herbstman, president at Settlement. 2020: Money locked in, shovels in the ground The development team closed on construction financing — which meant building could begin. This marked the end of the predevelopment timeline, which took two years — “pretty fast by today’s standards,” Lehman said. “Two years is roughly the minimum the project spends in predevelopment, but it could take longer depending on the specifics of the project and subsidy availability.” When the team closed, they signed a 99-year lease with NYCHA for the land, a process that included coordination with the federal Department of Housing and Urban Development. In the development world, leases set for 99 years are very common. The construction team started construction on closing day, in late December 2020. 2021: Construction continues The Covid-19 pandemic meant the construction team faced some challenges, but they ultimately finished on time despite unforeseen delays. Weiss, of Joy Construction, said starting in late 2020 meant the “initial craziness” of the Covid-19 pandemic had ebbed a bit. Though supply chains were snarled and shipping delays were common, the team had planned its supplies in advance and they were ready to arrive by the time the building’s foundation had been poured. And labor restrictions had eased up, too. “There were two sides to Covid,” Weiss said. “There was everything you read about labor shortages, but there also wasn’t a lot of construction going on in the city. There was less traffic in the city. I don’t want to say Covid was helpful, but I think it netted out.” Digging the foundation took about eight months, which was fairly typical for a project, Weiss said — even though challenges crept up during the excavation on The Bronx’s rocky ground. The team had to redesign the foundation because the soil was different than expected. The team also had to pay for a generator to power most of the construction work after Con Ed was unable to provide temporary power for many months. The generator’s gas was costly, Weiss said. After the foundation, the team constructed the building itself, topping off at 14 stories five or six months later. Another three to four months after that, the team enclosed the building, making sure it was weathertight, Weiss said. That allowed work to start on the interiors, including kitchens, bathrooms and floors. 2022: Marketing preparation As construction continued, Settlement began to prepare for marketing the apartments in the building as part of the housing lottery on Housing Connect. The team worked with HPD to prepare advertisements for how the building would be shown to potential tenants. 2023: Construction is substantially completed, and the housing lottery opens By February, applicants could apply to live in Twin Parks Terrace through the housing lottery on Housing Connect. There were 135 apartments priced for households making between $22,700 for one or two people, and up to $160,720 for a family of seven. In addition, 46 apartments were set aside for formerly homeless New Yorkers, who were referred to Settlement by HPD. “You get the list of people and start qualifying them so that people are ready to sign leases as soon as the building’s ready to open,” Herbstman said. “Then you continue qualifying households and signing leases after you get your temporary certificate of occupancy.” Meanwhile, as construction neared an end, the team began closing out permits with various agencies and other entities. For instance, it needed Con Ed to turn the utilities on and to get a certificate of occupancy inspection with the Buildings Department, a key step for a building to be tenant-ready. The development team in April received a temporary certificate of occupancy, which allowed residents to start moving into the building. DOB had to make sure the plumbing was up to snuff and elevators were safe, among other items. That same month, the lottery closed. By the fall, the first tenants started moving in. 2024: Tenants fill up the apartments. Residents continued moving in. 2025: The building reaches full occupancy After most of the tenants moved in and the building was operating for about three months, the team converted to permanent financing, which allowed them to pay down the construction loans and borrow with a lower interest rate while also unlocking more money for the project. The DOB issued the final certificate of occupancy in March. The process of moving from a temporary certificate of occupancy to the final version was all about paperwork, Weiss said: “It’s closing out the jobs.” Today Now, Twin Parks Terrace stands tall, wedged up a slope on a busy avenue. The building has play areas for children, laundry machines and bike storage. There’s a discount store on the ground floor, which also features another retail space for lease. On a weekday afternoon, individuals and families streamed in and out of the building. One of them was a tenant named Veronica Lopez. The sexagenarian moved into her one-bedroom apartment about three years ago, after seven years of applying to the housing lottery. “The apartments are beautiful. When I came in, I was the first one in my apartment,” Lopez said. “It was clean, new. Everything was perfect.” With a laugh she added, “It still is perfect because I have OCD.” Our nonprofit newsroom relies on donations from readers to sustain our local reporting and keep it free for all New Yorkers. items.originalTitle: My search for Bologna’s perfect tagliatelle al ragù - the real ‘spag bol’
items.author: Ben Aitken
items.title: My search for Bologna’s perfect tagliatelle al ragù - the real ‘spag bol’
items.summary: The signature dish of Italy’s gastronomic capital is taken far more seriously than its British derivative. So which restaurant does the best ‘tag rag’? I used to eat spag bol three times a week. I’d have it every Friday at my nan’s, every Saturday at my dad’s, and every Tuesday at my mum’s. My nan would lean heavily on Dolmio and add a cheeky splash of Tabasco. My mum would rustle up hers in the time it took the pasta to cook, which gave it a crunchiness that sometimes made me cry (I swear to God, those onions were practically raw). And my dad would let his bubble away for the duration of Gladiators, meaning that by the time it was dished up at the start of Blind Date, it had an intensity that felt positively foreign. I’m not alone in being a big fan of spag bol – the dish is often voted the nation’s favourite, and there’s now even a National Spaghetti Bolognese Day (22 May) – but I do sometimes wonder what it is about this relatively simple import, essentially a combo of mince and tomatoes plonked upon pasta, that has won over millions and withstood the vagaries of time. So I travelled to the dish’s motherland, Bologna, to unlock its secrets and hunt down some prime examples.

items.originalTitle: How To Apply for the NYC Housing Lottery
items.author: Samantha Maldonado
items.title: How To Apply for the NYC Housing Lottery
items.summary: Want to secure an affordable, rent-stabilized apartment through New York City’s housing lottery? Step right up and try your luck! As The City Reporter has shown, your chances of winning a subsidized apartment through the affordable lottery are a long shot, but not unheard of. In recent years, there has been one apartment available through the lottery for every 510 applications. Those lucky New Yorkers have a fabled, enviable opportunity: Moving into (typically) brand-new buildings with stabilized rent that’s likely cheaper than the market. But even when your number comes up in the lottery, there are a lot of hoops to jump through before you secure a lease. We spoke to leasing agents, city officials and some winners to find out the inside scoop on the lottery. Here’s our guide for locals on how to access those opportunities, tips to navigate the process and how you can prepare — with insight from people who won the lottery and professionals who screen applicants for lottery apartments. Read our full series on New York City’s affordable housing lottery. I’m Ready to Apply! Where Do I Start? You can sign up for and apply to housing lotteries on Housing Connect , a web-based system run through the city’s Department of Housing Preservation and Development that lists and manages all available subsidized apartments . Think of Housing Connect as the portal through which you enter lotteries for individual buildings. First, create a profile. You’ll include details about all sources of income, including from jobs, government assistance, investments or workers’ compensation, as well as the value of your assets in bank and investment accounts. You must include this income information for the people you’d live with. You’ll also indicate your current residence, whether it’s a rental, NYCHA building or a homeless shelter, and whether anyone you’re applying with receives rental assistance. Amira Willingham lives with her cat, Wulbren, in a Chelsea apartment she got through the housing lottery, June 26, 2026. Credit: Alex Krales/The City Reporter The information must be provided on the profile for each member of your household — that is, the people you’ll live with in that lottery apartment, not necessarily your current household. Make sure this information is complete, or else you won’t be able to submit an application. You can also include details about your preferences, such as interest in a ramp or elevator, number of bedrooms and a pet-friendly policy. One thing to keep in mind: “Anything you put on your profile, you will have to prove that it’s true,” said Wout Stienaers, a founder of Homey , a paid service that helps people apply to the housing lottery. “Don’t lie about anything.” For instance, Stienaers said applicants might be tempted to say they have a disability because there are apartments set aside for those who do (more on that later). But you’d be asked to provide proof of that disability, like a letter from a doctor. You can get free help to apply for the housing lottery through HPD’s Housing Ambassador Program . I Made a Profile on Housing Connect. Now What? Once you’ve made a profile, check buildings for which you’re eligible and click “Apply Now.” You’ll know if you’re eligible if your household income falls within a range based on the number of people you’ll be living with. (How is that income range determined? Read our guide on that here.) Keep the information about your household and income updated as you go along. For example: If you or your partner get a raise or lose a job, make sure to log that information. If you become a parent, add your child as a member of your household! One caveat: don’t change your household size after you apply to a lottery. “If a household is a single mom and a teenager, and then they find out they only qualify for a studio, they can’t then add the grandmother with Social Security income to see if they qualify for another unit,” said Christine Wendell, CEO of Pront Housing, an affordable housing leasing company. “If they try to do that, they will be rejected, so they should just pick their household size, and stick with it.” MORE: What Is ‘Affordable Housing’ in New York, and What Are My Options? Make sure to check back on Housing Connect frequently, as new opportunities come online often. Application periods for each building are open for two months. It doesn’t matter when you submit your application within that period, as long as you apply before the lottery closes. “No matter at what point in time you submit your application, you have the same chance to win as everybody else,” Stienaers said. Don’t be shy about throwing your hat in the ring! You can apply to as many lotteries as you’re eligible for. “You can apply to an unlimited number of buildings,” Wendell said. “Just statistically speaking, you will have a greater chance of getting an affordable housing unit if you apply to a lot of buildings, which everyone is completely allowed to do.” How Can I know if I’m Eligible? To be eligible for affordable housing through Housing Connect, your household income must fall within a specific band. Your household’s assets must also fall under a certain amount. The asset limits vary based on building and requirements. That means if you have a lot of savings or holdings in a stock portfolio, you may not be eligible for the lottery, even if your income falls within the bands. Can I Apply With a Voucher or Rental Subsidy? Yes! If you get rental assistance through programs including Section 8, CityFHEPS or Medicaid Waiver, you’re good, and then you’re not subject to minimum income requirements. But the amount of rent of the apartment you’re applying to must be within the limits of what your voucher covers. “If you have a voucher, you should apply for everything because your income isn’t your limiting factor anymore,” said Michelle de la Uz, executive director at the nonprofit Fifth Avenue Committee. “It’s basically whatever your voucher is approved for.” That means as a voucher-holder, you may be eligible to apply for more housing lotteries than you think. Even if you don’t make enough money, you can apply for apartments based on the amount of rent — as long as it’s no more than what your voucher is worth. Can People Apply to the Lottery if They Don’t Live in New York City? Yes, they technically can, but applicants who are New York City residents get priority. “While any and everybody can apply for Housing Connect lotteries, it first focuses on folks that reside within the five boroughs of New York City before it can move someone that does not reside in New York City into one of its apartments,” said Shaheem Taylor, a marketing outreach coordinator at HPD, in a webinar . It’s very rare for outside applicants to secure an apartment through a lottery. A New York City resident who applies to the lottery is over 10 times more likely to sign a lease for an affordable apartment than someone who lives outside the city, according to an analysis of HPD data by The City Reporter. MORE: What Are Your Odds of Winning NYC’s Affordable Housing Lottery? Having set his sights on someday moving back to his birthplace of New York City, Grayson Sparrow applied to housing lotteries from his home in Virginia. He lucked out when he moved back to the city in April 2024 and was asked to submit his documents for a housing lottery building in East New York just three months later. “I’d been applying just in the event if I move back someday and maybe it lines up with something,” Sparrow, 30, said. “My info went in and by the time they pulled it, I had New York residency.” Can I Apply to the Lottery for a Rental Apartment if I Own Property? If you or a member of your household own property within 100 miles of New York City, then you can’t apply through the lottery. (And you can’t try for an affordable homeownership lottery if you own, or ever owned, property anywhere.) Can I Apply for One Lottery Multiple Times? No! One entry per household. Your household means all the people who will live in the apartment you’ll be applying to. Only one member of the household should apply for the lottery. And you can’t apply for the same lottery twice, even if, for example, you’re applying with a roommate and then on your own. If more than one member of a household applies to the lottery, the application is automatically disqualified. Christina Harsch, director of leasing and compliance at Wavecrest Management, recommends keeping track of what you’re applying to and the information you’re sending in, if you get your number called. “Keep a journal of what you’re applying to and when you apply, keep copies of the [Housing Connect] ad if you can and even copies of applications so you remember what you’re doing,” she said. That way, you know your household only applies to one lottery and you can follow up with the agents if need be. Need more help? Connect with a housing ambassador to get assistance preparing for and applying to the housing lottery. What Else Might Improve My Chances of Being Selected? If you work for the city government, are a military veteran or live in the same neighborhood as the building you’re applying for, you might get a boost in the lottery. That’s because a percentage of the available apartments are set aside for people who fall under specific categories. In all new buildings, 5% of apartments are for households where a member has a mobility disability and 2% for households where a member has a hearing or vision disability. In addition, 10% of apartments are set aside for city employees and military veterans, and 20% for residents of the community district where the building is located. Some projects offer preferences for seniors or formerly homeless individuals, as well. OK I Entered a Lottery! How Long Will It Take Before I Hear Back? Once you apply, you get assigned a random number called a log number. The lower it is, the better chance you have of being contacted for the development. And then it could be weeks, months or years before you hear back if your number has been selected. Some people never hear back, even if they are eligible! Others don’t hear anything for a long time, but all of a sudden, will be notified their number was chosen for multiple buildings. Pro tip: Make sure to stay on top of your Housing Connect account so you don’t miss any notifications. Taylor, of HPD, recommends applicants check their Housing Connect account three times a week. Jumelia Abrahamson, director of programs at University Neighborhood Housing Program, said she tells people to log into Housing Connect “as often as you’re logging into your social media.” She also tells applicants to check their email on a daily basis. “Leasing agents are not calling, they’re not texting, and if these communications are going into the junk mail or if people don’t check their emails on a daily basis, they’re missing a lot of communication,” she said. (If you applied on paper, you can choose whether to get notifications via email or in your actual mailbox — but ideally, you’ve applied through Housing Connect! Otherwise, it can be a slower process.) What’s the Status of My Lottery Application? Housing Connect will indicate where your application is in the process. Here’s what those statuses mean, according to experts: Pending just means you submitted your application. Nothing else! Action required means there is a request for documentation, indicating you moved to the next stage in the process — your log number was pulled — and you need to respond to a request from the lottery administrators. (If you happen to be rejected, that will also appear under “action required.”) In process could mean one of two things: either that you submitted your documents and they are under review, or you missed the window to submit the documents. Completed indicates the end stage of the application process. It can mean that you signed a lease and received your keys. Or it could mean there are no more apartments available in a development. Or it could mean you were rejected in the process and did not appeal the rejection within the required timeline. My Number Got Picked! Now What? Once you’re notified your number was called in a lottery, get ready for a long road. This is where the process can get tricky, as you must provide a pile of paperwork to verify your eligibility, including identifications and proof of income. You have 10 business days to submit those documents. And if the leasing agent requests more documents beyond what was in your original application, an applicant has five business days to respond. “Five days is really not a long time if you’re not checking, and once that five days is gone, your place in line has been passed by,” said Charmaine Marizan, the affordable housing marketing and leasing manager at Fifth Avenue Committee. “If you don’t get back quickly, there’s a bunch of people who need it.” It’s good to get as many of your documents in order as you can before you’re selected, experts say. Keep a digital file of PDFs of important information so you can send it off quickly if your number is called. Here is a list of the documents you may need to provide. In sum, you must provide IDs — such as IDNYC, drivers’ license, or state ID card — for all members of the household, plus birth certificates for minors. You’ll need to show all sources of income so the agent can verify you qualify within the income bands. That includes interest from assets, student loans, child support payments and even regular checks or Venmo payments from family members or others. Applicants employed by jobs must submit a month of pay stubs, and self-employed applicants must provide tax returns. New residential housing in the South Bronx was located near the 149th Street-Third Avenue transit hub, July 20, 2026. Credit: Ben Fractenberg/The City Reporter If you get benefits through SNAP, TANF or Social Security, you can simply submit the income determination you got through those programs. You’ll also have to show your assets, if you have more than $51,600 saved and in investment accounts. That means providing bank account and retirement account statements, among other records. If you have less than that $51,600 in assets, you can just self-certify that that’s the case — no need to prove it. Once it’s confirmed that you’re eligible for an apartment — and there’s a vacancy available — you can either show you’ve paid rent for the past year, or you can opt for a credit check. There’s no application fee, but you might be charged $20 for a background or credit check. You might have a back-and-forth with the listing agent who represents the development. They may ask for more information or clarification. You can also ask them questions. Amira Willingham, 25, who won her Chelsea studio through the lottery, said the agent asked her about specific transactions on her bank account. “I had to explain to them every transaction,” she said. “I bought a lot online so I had lots of receipts to show.” On one occasion, Willingham had to get a copy of a friend’s bank statement with everything blacked out except a transaction showing Willingham sending the friend money for a dinner. “There’s no privacy in the process,” Willingham said. “I wish I had known to have a folder of everything I’d ever done put together and up to date.” When she wasn’t sure about how to move forward, Willingham turned to an online forum she found helpful to chat with others navigating the process. Dan B., a musician who lives in a Greenpoint apartment he won through the lottery, advised following up with the agent to get clarity on requirements and to check in for updates: “You really have to advocate for yourself because no one’s going to care more about you getting it than yourself.” And when you advocate for yourself, it’s good to stick to email when contacting agents in order to maintain a record, said Mildred Flores, director of affordable housing marketing and compliance at Settlement Housing Fund. “Everybody’s going to do things differently. There are some marketing agents that terminate applications as quickly as they can, and then there are others that you know will work with applicants,” Flores said. She said she typically tells applicants to wait to contact agents for a status update until 30 days have passed since the start of tenant selection. Have patience, she cautioned, as agents often are working to lease up multiple buildings at a time and handling hundreds of applications. For those who inquire, Flores said she will give applicants a sense of their chances and the timeline based on their log numbers — again, the random number assigned to you when you enter a lottery. I Got Turned Down. What Can I Do? You can appeal the decision. Within five days of the decision, write to the agent to say why you think you should not have been rejected, or why you think you should still be moving forward, and send in supporting documents. “An applicant can appeal at any part in the process, except during the initial qualification period,” Flores said. If an applicant successfully appeals, they will not lose their place in the queue. The Atlantic Chestnut Complex in Cypress Hills, Brooklyn, provided affordable housing units, May 7, 2026. Credit: Ben Fractenberg/The City Reporter HPD is not involved in this process — it’s the agents associated with the building who handle the appeals. Often, applicants face rejection because they don’t meet income or household eligibility requirements, because a single household submitted more than one application for a building or because there was insufficient information provided to the leasing agent. Willingham said she appealed at least three times during the process when agents disqualified her based on insufficient information or not providing the right documentations. “I had to kind of be a Karen about it,” she said. “This is one of the only paths to affordable housing in the city. Doing anything you can to fight to get it is really important.” I Got Approved. What’s Next? You’ll likely take a tour of the apartment — or multiple open apartments in one new complex — and if you like what you see, you can decide to move forward. You’ll have 30 days to accept a lease offer or complete a purchase, if it’s a lottery homeownership opportunity. You’ll have to pay the first month’s rent and a security deposit (equal to a month’s rent) upfront, so make sure you have savings! You’ll also have to figure out how to get out of your current lease, sometimes with limited notice. That requires negotiating with your landlord. How Long Will This Whole Process Take? It can vary a ton! The answer has to do with how fast you as the applicant are able to mobilize, and what kind of obstacles may pop up in the screening process. Between July 1, 2025, and June 30, 2026, the median time it took for an applicant to get approved for an apartment after the lottery ended was 136 days (about 4.5 months). For Sparrow, who had applied to the housing lottery from outside New York, a year passed between when he applied for the building and when leasing agents reached out to ask for documents. Three months after that, he signed the lease for his affordable apartment. “It is a little surprising how my process was seamless,” he said. “I’ve seen other people where they get asked for documents and it takes months for them to move into the apartment.” WIllingham, on the other hand, applied for her building’s lottery in February of one year, received a request for documents by November, and moved in the following March. What Happens if My Life Changes Between When I Get a Call for the Lottery? That can happen — and it’s why you should keep your Housing Connect profile updated. If your life changes between when you apply for a lottery and your number gets picked, you get screened for your current situation. Maybe you got married and had a family, or maybe you got promoted. Either way, you may or may not qualify for the apartment any more. The agent will work with you to figure it out. But be careful! You don’t want your situation to change during the screening process. Marizan, for instance, cautions against earning too much overtime, which can alter your income. “If you’re currently in the screening process and you’re due a promotion, hold back on it,” she said. “You cannot be over-income by a penny.” Any Other Way to Secure Affordable Housing? Yup: look for apartments that people won through the lottery but are now vacant.They’re called re-rentals (or re-sales, for homeownership). These kinds of apartments don’t go through the lottery — at least until April 30, 2027 . That means you can apply for these affordable apartments almost like any other apartment — essentially, first-come, first-served. You can find listings here and here , or on the sites of individual property management companies. StreetEasy, Zillow and other listings sites may also feature vacant affordable housing re-rentals. Harsch, of Wavecrest Management, suggested reaching out to affordable management companies by cold-calling or emailing to ask about their re-rental stock. (She mentioned even if there’s nothing to offer, she may add people who get in touch to a mailing list and send them info about new housing opportunities.) If you apply for a re-rental opportunity, you still must be eligible for the apartment based on your income and household size — details that the leasing agent will need to verify. So it takes time! And they may add you to a wait list that they’ll pull from if another applicant doesn’t work out. items.originalTitle: ‘The currency competition is now a software competition’: Why Japan’s banks think digital currencies give the yen a boost
items.author: Angelica Ang
items.title: ‘The currency competition is now a software competition’: Why Japan’s banks think digital currencies give the yen a boost
items.summary: Currencies such as the Japanese yen or the euro have tried and failed to loosen the U.S. dollar’s grip on world trade , unable to outweigh the U.S.’s deep and open financial markets. But now, Japanese bankers think that the rise of digital currencies could give the yen a new path to worldwide use. “The currency competition is now a software competition,” Tomoya Hasebe, global head of digital and innovation at Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC), said at a roundtable in Singapore on Nov. 16. “Currency dominance is increasingly determined not only by central bank policy or regulatory policy, but by which currency is easiest to use as code.” The yen is the world’s third most-used currency, after the U.S. dollar and the euro. Japan was the first country among G7 economies to roll out a comprehensive framework to regulate stablecoins. Yet yen-pegged stablecoins have barely enjoyed much usage, with U.S. dollar-denominated stablecoins accounting for more than 97% of the market . The country’s three megabanks—Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group, and the Mizuho Financial Group—are planning to change that with a jointly-issued yen-backed stablecoin set to begin transactions next March . The new stablecoin is meant to streamline cross-border payments and boost the appeal of the yen for global business. Several Asian economies are rolling out their own stablecoins to cater to firms seeking alternatives to the U.S. dollar. Hong Kong, for example, issued its first two Hong Kong dollar-backed stablecoin issuer licenses in April , to HSBC and Anchorpoint Financial, a joint venture by Standard Chartered Bank, HKT, and Web3 firm Animoca Brands. “The majority of global trade is still in USD, but there is certainly a group of firms around the world that want to not use U.S. dollars for trade,” said Tim Way, senior director of global banking at digital asset infrastructure firm Fireblocks. “It’s an opportunity for Asia to stand up and have more trade in Asia running in Asian currencies.” Startups are entering a financial ecosystem that’s long been dominated by incumbents. JPYC, a Japanese startup, launched the country’s first yen-pegged stablecoin in October 2025. “More private enterprises and start-ups are starting to enter the stablecoin area,” Makoto Shibata, the head of Finolab, a Japanese fintech accelerator, said. Yet, it remains to be seen if yen-backed stablecoins—whether by on-chain start-ups or trad-fi institutions—will be able to gain traction. Unlike U.S. dollar stablecoins that generate returns from high-yielding treasury bills, yen-pegged stablecoins operate on razor-thin margins. Since JPYC was founded in 2019, it has faced steep growth bottlenecks , as users frequently redeem the token for traditional fiat, rather than hold it in their digital wallets. items.author: Phuong Le
items.title: Accidents, emotional affairs and impromptu Leonard Cohen dancing - My Wife Cries review
items.summary: Angela Schanelec’s famously uncompromising work takes on a new warmth in this sometimes playful study of everyday emotional turmoil The elliptical cinema of German film-maker Angela Schanelec is often described as uncompromising. This latest work, however, radiates a striking warmth. We see a marriage tearing at the seams, but this untethering is devoid of the usual dramatic flourishes. On an ordinary day like any another, construction worker Thomas (Vladimir Vulevic) notices a missed call from his wife, Carla (Agathe Bonitzer); when he phones back, she doesn’t pick up. The event holds little significance for the mild-mannered man; he carries on his usual chitchat with his co-workers, mundane catchups that unfold over static, tableaux-like shots. This deceptive calm is ruptured, however, when Thomas finds Carla sobbing helplessly on a park bench. A seismic change has taken hold within her: she will later confide in him of an emotional affair, and a tragic accident that leaves her emotionally unmoored. These revelations surface not through screaming matches, but by way of protracted conversations that resemble monologues rather than actual dialogue. Similar sequences recur as we are introduced to the rest of the couple’s social orbit, each of whom are wrestling with their own internal changes. There’s an enigmatic blend of theatricality and cinematic wizardry here; these wordy contemplations often occur when characters are on the move, walking, cycling or simply wandering about. There’s a subtle physicality and tactility to their inner struggles.
