items.originalTitle: What is Area Median Income? The Magic Number Behind Affordable Housing Math in NYC
items.author: Samantha Maldonado
items.title: What is Area Median Income? The Magic Number Behind Affordable Housing Math in NYC
items.summary: A Murray Hill two-bedroom for $4,518. A Marble Hill one-bedroom for $3,180. A Flatbush studio for $2,022. These were some recent affordable housing offerings in the city’s lottery system . But those rents aren’t exactly cheap. You might ask, affordable for whom? In New York City, affordable housing — at least what’s in the housing lottery — is housing where the rent is set at about one-third of household income and receives some sort of government subsidy. The affordable housing in the lottery is rent-stabilized, meaning its price can increase only in increments as approved by the Rent Guidelines Board. But affordable housing is not necessarily housing only for low-income people. “Affordable housing is for all income levels and sizes,” said Shaheem Taylor, a lottery marketing outreach coordinator at the Department of Housing Preservation and Development, during a Housing Connect webinar earlier this year. “Regardless of whether you make $10,000, $0, six figures, $50,000 — there are lotteries that are allocated to everyone.” Read on to understand why some of the city’s affordable housing may appear rather expensive, and what it means for your Housing Connect application: Read our full series on New York City’s affordable housing lottery. Table of contents How the Rent Is Set: Understanding AMI, or Area Median Income Why Are Some ‘Affordable’ Apartments So Expensive? Lowest Rents, Biggest Squeeze If ‘Affordable’ Apartments Are So Expensive, What’s the Point of Trying To Get One? Who Decides On Levels of Affordability and Why? How the Rent Is Set: Understanding AMI, or Area Median Income Affordable housing in New York City may be tied to your household’s income, but the measure used to determine an affordable building’s income categories is based on a federally set figure that’s based on rents, not the actual money a household earns. Confused? Stick with us, because that figure — the area median income, or AMI — is really important to understanding your next application to New York’s housing lottery. Each year, the federal Department of Housing and Urban Development sets the area median income, or AMI, for the New York City area, which includes the five boroughs as well as Putnam, Rockland, and Westchester counties. The AMI is a federal measure based on rents in the area, not on actual household earnings. Elsewhere, AMI is based on actual incomes, but in our area, HUD considers rent in the calculation because with high housing costs, more people — at higher incomes — would need access to affordable housing. There is one AMI for the whole city, so the AMI for, say, the Upper East Side or Riverdale is the same for Elmhurst or Brownsville. Why is the AMI so important? Because when beginning to develop new affordable housing, the city housing agency creates categories of income ranges as a percentage of the AMI, then sets the rents based on them. (Remember, affordable housing means residents spend no more than 30% of their income on housing costs.) That’s why on Housing Connect, you see listings that say things like, applicants for a certain apartment must not earn more than, let’s say, 60% of the area median income, or 100% of the area median income. The AMI is the maximum a household is allowed to earn for a given affordable apartment, with rents pegged to be no more than 30% of that number. So what does that look like? Here’s where the AMI is set in 2026 : 100% of New York’s AMI was $118,800 for an individual and $169,600 for a family of four. 30% of the AMI was $35,640 for an individual and $50,880 for a family of four. 130% of the AMI was $154,440 for an individual and $220,480 for a family of four. If those numbers look high to you — remember, they do not reflect actual incomes in New York City. They reflect market-rate rents in city and nearby counties. Based on census data, the actual median income for a household in New York City is about $81,000 . A family of three with that income would fall somewhere between 50% and 60% of the AMI. Why Are Some ‘Affordable’ Apartments So Expensive? Remember how AMI in the New York City area reflects rents rather than actual incomes? The thinking behind that, as HUD sees it, is because rent is so expensive here that more people across a wider range of incomes should be eligible for affordable housing. But it also can mean that sometimes the affordable housing is not exactly accessible for lower-income New Yorkers — and the prices can rival traditional, market-rate units for potential tenants who have higher incomes. Chris Walters, a land use policy coordinator at nonprofit Association for Neighborhood and Housing Development, pointed out that as the AMI figures rise each year, so do the rents for affordable apartments. “As the AMI numbers have increased every year, at the higher end you start to get into rents that border on market-rate in some neighborhoods, or even exceed them,” Walters said. That means rents go up at both the top income levels and at the bottom, which means the rents can feel out of reach for the lowest-earning households. Let’s look at some numbers. Housing Connect advertised a studio for $2,022 in Flatbush — reserved for people making 80% AMI, or between $75,772.00 to $95,040 for an individual. It’s a new building with air conditioning, a dishwasher and in-unit laundry. But on the same block, you could find a studio on the open market listed for $1,875. It’s in a pre-war elevator building and lacks the previous amenities, but there are no income restrictions. North of there, in Crown Heights, one building on Housing Connect offered two-bedrooms for $4,518 — affordable at 130% of AMI, or for a family of four earning between $162,446 and $220,480. A two-bedroom apartment in the same building that’s not considered affordable is listed on the open market for about $5,000. But a household looking for a two-bedroom just a couple blocks away could find one on the market for $2,750 or $3,300 . Lowest Rents, Biggest Squeeze Because affordable housing means paying about a third of income towards rent, what that means in practice feels different for different household budgets. Take a household that makes $100,000 a year. That family would pay about $30,000 annually for rent, with $70,000 left over for other expenses. But if a household makes $45,000 and pays $13,500 annually for rent, that household has just $31,500 left over for all other expenses. “There’s a big discrepancy between what’s left over for everything else, and that can also make something feel less affordable even if it is ‘affordable,’” said Emily Kurtz, chief housing officer at affordable housing provider RiseBoro Community Partnership. That math may change, if City Hall under Mayor Zohran Mamdani keeps its promise. His administration in May committed to changing the calculation for rent in affordable housing for New Yorkers at the lowest income levels. For those at 30% of AMI — or $50,880 for a family of four — the rent will be set at no more than a quarter of household income. That’d be around $1,060 per month for that family. If ‘Affordable’ Apartments Are So Expensive, What’s the Point of Trying To Get One? Some New Yorkers may see the rents of some lottery units and say, no thanks, that’s not a deal. But experts point out that affordable apartments are rent stabilized, so while the rent may be expensive in the first year or two, it won’t grow at the same rate as market-rate rents could. Over time, that really adds up. “The value of having regulated apartments is that the rents stay relatively low as income grows, as other rents grow. But year one, your rent might feel very tight,” Kurtz said. Also: Rent-stabilized tenants have some of the strongest rights against eviction in the country. Who Decides On Levels of Affordability and Why? Developers take multiple factors into consideration as they plan their affordable housing projects. It’s a complicated process because each financing source has different restrictions based on what kind of housing is being developed. Developers can also take advantage of incentives, whether tax abatements or being allowed to build bigger, in exchange for including a certain number of affordable apartments for prescribed income levels And lots of affordable housing is subsidized, meaning the government throws in taxpayer funding. A new residential building in Park Slope had affordable units available through the housing lottery, Nov. 12, 2026. Credit: Screengrab via Housing Connect “You start to layer, and that’s why affordable housing is so complex, because you’re layering, layering, layering to get as many sources as you can so that you can have very low-income units and workforce housing units,” Kurtz said. Apartments set at lower rents need more subsidy, and HPD must figure out how to use its money to balance creating as many affordable apartments as possible. Developers must consider how much it costs not only to build the project, but also to operate and maintain them as costs — like insurance and utilities — rise. Developers must make sure the projects pencil out. In other words, the math needs to math. Developers also consider the project’s income. The lower the affordability — so AMIs of, say, 30% or 50% instead of 100% or higher — the more limited the rental income a developer can take in. Taking in more rent means the project can take on more private debt and lean less on public subsidy. And the opposite is true: when a project becomes more affordable to renters it usually needs more public subsidy. Public subsidies are limited, and require tough choices. “It’s a public policy decision of how to use subsidy resources and and how to both make those go as far as possible, but also reach the levels of deep affordability that the city clearly needs,” said Patrick Boyle, senior policy director at Enterprise Community Partners. “Reaching lower-income people and making housing affordable to residents takes more subsidy. That’s the trade-off in the calculation.” Our nonprofit newsroom relies on donations from readers to sustain our local reporting and keep it free for all New Yorkers. Donate to THE CITY today. items.originalTitle: Rural voters revolted because they wanted Republicans to help them. GOP didn’t deliver
items.title: Rural voters revolted because they wanted Republicans to help them. GOP didn’t deliver
items.summary: Rural counties swung more than 15 percentage points toward Democrats in the 2026 midterms . Republicans lost rural strongholds including Iowa, South Carolina, and Kansas, where a Democrat won a U.S. Senate seat for the first time since 1932. Republicans haven’t fully lost rural America, but they got one heck of a warning. Just before the election, a national survey of rural voters found that about 75% rated their local cost of living as fair or poor. Nearly half worried about making their rent or mortgage payments. FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS The GOP doesn't need another consultant's postmortem to understand what happened. It needs to look at what's happening to the people who feed, build and power this country. Farm production expenses are projected to reach nearly $493 billion in 2026, up 4.5% in a single year, while inflation-adjusted net farm income is expected to fall 5.5%. In 2012, John Deere's flagship combine cost roughly $454,000, when wheat was $7.77 a bushel. Today, its flagship combine costs over $1.1 million, while wheat is projected at $6.91 a bushel. Meanwhile, family farm bankruptcies jumped 46% in 2025. BROOKE ROLLINS, MONICA CROWLEY: AMERICA’S FAMILY FARMS HAVE KEPT US STRONG FOR 250 YEARS Ranchers are seeing record cattle prices, but production costs have climbed nearly 30% since 2020. Ranchers also face a government-enabled meatpacking oligopoly where four companies account for roughly 85% of steer and heifer purchases. Federal regulations make opening independent processing facilities prohibitively expensive, leaving ranchers with fewer buyers and little negotiating power. CUT THE BULL: THE REAL REASON BEEF COSTS SO MUCH — AND WHAT TRUMP IS TRYING TO DO Washington's response to agricultural hardship increasingly involves writing checks. Direct government farm payments are projected to reach $47.4 billion this year. Assistance can keep operations alive, but subsidies don't make equipment cheaper or create new markets. Too often, that money flows straight through farmers to banks, lenders, equipment manufacturers and chemical suppliers. Farmers become little more than conduits for taxpayer dollars, collecting a government check with one hand and handing it over to the industries squeezing them with the other. Counterintuitively, tariffs have increased costs for imported machinery, steel and agricultural inputs while exposing American exports to retaliation. Farmers are expected to compete globally while the tools of competition get more expensive. AMERICAN BUSINESSES AREN’T ALLOWED TO BUILD. IT’S TIME CONGRESS HELPED THEM The timber industry has fared just as poorly. In 1988, America's national forests produced 12.6 billion board feet of timber. By 2024, that figure had collapsed to just 2.7 billion, a 79% decline. Federal regulations, bureaucratic roadblocks and relentless litigation have strangled timber production, shuttered sawmills and devastated communities that depended on these jobs for generations. Adding insult to injury, federal law can even force taxpayers to foot the legal bills for environmental groups that successfully sue to block timber projects. Meanwhile, millions of acres have gone up in flames across America this year, while the sawmills that once turned those trees into lumber sit shuttered in towns now choking on wildfire smoke from timber that used to build American homes. Republicans promised to take a chainsaw to federal bureaucracy. Instead, chainsaws are sitting idle as timber mills rust into the ground. The Trump administration deserves credit for proposing to repeal Clinton’s 2001 Roadless Rule. But the repeal remains unfinished and would only scratch the surface of what is needed to reignite our timber industry. Along with timber, America needs domestic copper, silver and critical minerals to power its future and create high-paying jobs. Yet it takes nearly 29 years to open a new mine, longer than anywhere in the world except Zambia. Coal production is projected to fall 2% in 2026. Even with record American oil production, diesel is expected to average $5.25 a gallon. Coal towns face declining production while farmers and truckers pay a fortune for fuel. A Republican trifecta was supposed to deliver American energy dominance. But while D.C. loves the products of rural industry, it stands in the way of the industries themselves. AMERICA'S TRUCKERS ISSUE DIRE WARNING AS SOARING DIESEL COSTS THREATEN 'DOMINO EFFECT' Take all this bureaucracy, overregulation, and financial hardship together, and it’s no wonder Republicans heard a harsh rebuke from rural America on Election Day . In 2024, voters who described themselves as financially struggling favored President Donald Trump by roughly 30 points. In 2026, voters describing the same circumstances favored Democrats by approximately 30 points. MEHEK COOKE: REPUBLICANS FAILED THE AFFORDABILITY TEST. THIS IS HOW TO WIN VOTERS BACK Republicans have made real progress on tax reform, preventing one of the largest tax increases in American history and proposing meaningful regulatory reforms. But preventing a tax increase doesn't make diesel or fertilizer cheaper. Proposing regulatory reform isn't the same as delivering it. And families struggling to make ends meet aren't interested in hearing how much worse things could have been. Republicans shouldn't mistake the midterms for rural America suddenly embracing socialist economic policies . The warning is simpler: people are frustrated with the cost of living, disappearing opportunities and a political system better at managing their problems than solving them. The answer isn’t more government, it's freedom. Republicans need to start acting like the party that believes in it. Keep fighting for tax cuts, American innovation and fiscal responsibility. Those battles matter. But it's time to listen to congressional Republicans who actually represent rural America and understand what’s needed to revive the communities that put the GOP in power cycle after cycle. Start by passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, now before the Senate, to reform the Endangered Species Act and overhaul federal permitting . Reform the Equal Access to Justice Act so taxpayers aren't footing the legal bills for groups that sue to block logging, mining and energy development. items.originalTitle: In Hakeem Jeffries’ Rise to Speaker, Black Leaders See a Milestone—and a Test
items.author: Philip Wang
items.title: In Hakeem Jeffries’ Rise to Speaker, Black Leaders See a Milestone—and a Test
items.summary: Rep. Hakeem Jeffries speaks at a rally on extending Obamacare subsidies on the steps of the U.S. Capitol on Dec. 18, 2025, in Washington, DC. —Chip Somodevilla—Getty Images In 1870, Joseph Rainey of South Carolina became the first Black person to serve in the U.S. House. This week, current and newly elected House Democrats are poised to meet to select Rep. Hakeem Jeffries as the chamber’s first Black Speaker. It is a moment fraught with meaning and hurdles for both the New York Democrat and the larger Black community, multiple Black leaders tell TIME. They spoke of the symbolic significance of Jeffries taking on a role that puts him second in the presidential line of succession as well as the challenge of turning a breakthrough in Black representation into policies that actually improve voters’ lives. “When Martin Luther King Jr. said, ‘I have a dream,’ he's saying it's deeply rooted in the American dream, and that's the tradition that Congressman Jeffries taps into,” says Rev. Frederick Haynes, a pastor at a Black megachurch who was just elected to a U.S. House seat in Dallas . As Speaker, Jeffries will set the legislative priorities for the House and play a central role in negotiations over federal spending and policy. He will also help lead his party’s opposition against a Trump administration that has spent much of the past two years dismantling institutions intended to protect Americans’ civil rights , as well as a President who earlier this year shared a video portraying Barack and Michelle Obama as apes. Democrats are set to have their biggest majority since the opening years of Obama’s presidency. The moment carries echoes of 2008, when Obama’s election broke a racial barrier while raising expectations that Democrats would deliver economic relief and lasting change. For Rep. Jim Clyburn, a South Carolina Democrat and one of the most influential Black lawmakers in the country, Jeffries’ task is to advance the party’s agenda while maintaining the trust of his caucus. In an interview with TIME, he says the advice he’s given Jeffries is private, but describes the tenor of much of it in a single sentence: “Conduct yourself in such a way that you'll ensure that you won't be the last.” Jeffries has been teed up for this job ever since 2022, when House Democrats, then in the minority, selected him to replace Nancy Pelosi as their next leader. Long before this month’s midterm elections, he had already won the support of the Congressional Black Caucus as well as key progressive members such as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Greg Casar , the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus. Yet some progressives remain skeptical of his selection, arguing that he is the wrong leader for the moment. Since Election Day, several incoming progressive members have said they remain uncommitted to backing Jeffries as Speaker, and some liberal groups have called for someone else to lead the chamber. Clyburn, who has been a mentor to Jeffries for years, suggests the Speaker role can often feel thankless, as so much of it involves managing different party factions and personalities without bruising egos. “You're operating behind a glass door,” he says. “Everybody thereby can see through.” Rep. James Clyburn speaks with Jeffries on Jan. 15, 2024 at Zion Baptist Church during a celebration of Martin Luther King Jr. —Tracy Glantz—The State/Tribune News Service via Getty Images In an open letter to his colleagues released earlier this month after historic wins in the midterm, Jeffries wrote that he intended to draw upon “the insights and perspectives of every single part of the Caucus in the days and weeks ahead.” But he also made clear that the expectations for him and his party are to do more than deliver messaging bills or score political points. “House Democrats must deliver dramatic change,” he wrote. Jeffries’ root in the Black church Haynes recalled first meeting Jeffries years ago and coming away impressed. It was at Cornerstone Baptist Church in Brooklyn, which Haynes regularly visited as a guest preacher. Cornerstone was an essential organizing hub for the Civil Rights Movement and had a close relationship with Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Jeffries attended the church while growing up in the Crown Heights neighborhood. “There are some people when you meet them and they're young, you know they have the ‘it’ factor,” Haynes says of Jeffries. “You know that they are hungry for knowledge. They are determined to make a difference.” Haynes is now one of several religious leaders poised to join Congress in January. Others include incoming Senators Adam Hamilton of Kansas, a lead pastor at a megachurch, and James Talarico of Texas, who is a seminarian. Haynes suggests Jeffries’ ascendance is also part of that trend, as he sees an opportunity for Jeffries to bring forth the best of the Black church tradition front and center. “Congressman Jeffries will have an opportunity to bring the moral tradition of the Black community that has believed in democracy, even when we've been victimized by a practice of democracy that was more fascist than democratic,” he says. “You cannot appreciate what it means to be black in this country without knowing that our community has always believed in democracy.” Turning representation into results Perhaps no one understands the challenges Jeffries is about to face better than Carl Heastie , who is the first Black Speaker of the New York Assembly, a role he’s held since 2015. Heastie has known Jeffries for decades, and worked with him when Jeffries was a member of the State Assembly from 2007 to 2012. Heastie says that being a speaker means balancing the roles of leader and legislator. It requires listening first to your constituents, but also to your colleagues, who are counting on you to manage both the chamber and your party’s caucus. It also means allowing his real-life experiences as a Black person to shape his decisions as both a lawmaker and speaker when appropriate, he says. He highlighted Jeffries’ work helping secure a 2010 state law involving how New York counted incarcerated people for state and local redistricting. It's a practice that disproportionately impacts the state’s Black population. The law required that incarcerated people by counted in their home communities. In the State Assembly, Jeffries led a passionate debate on why counting people where they are incarcerated, also known as prison gerrymandering , not only violates the rights of incarcerated people but also disenfranchises communities without a prison. “Hakeem to me was always one of the finer debaters on the floor,” Heastie says. “When he debated or spoke on the bill, everybody would stop what they were doing to make sure that you listened to him.” Heastie describes Jeffries’ expected promotion as more than just a moment of pride for his friend and former colleague. It suggests that, despite “terrible times and terrible dispositions,” the American dream remains very much alive. “That a Black person from Brooklyn can become the first Black Speaker in the history of this nation,” Heastie says. “I'm just so proud of him, and I can't wait.”
